title: How to Handle Money in an Affluent Society
excerpt: Jesus said more about money than almost anything else, and almost none of it is comfortable for the comfortable. Handling money well begins by admitting how much it already handles you.
body:
Jesus talked about money constantly, and the comfortable have learned to read past it the way we read past the prophets on the poor. You cannot serve God and money, he said, naming wealth as a rival god with a will of its own, not a neutral tool. He told a rich young ruler to sell what he had. He warned that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom. He told a story about a man who built bigger barns and died the night he finished. The pattern is unmistakable, and it is aimed straight at us, because by the measure of history and the world, we are the rich young ruler.

The first honest move is to admit that money is not just sitting in your account. It is shaping your fears, your sense of security, your status, and your sleep. In an affluent society, the danger is not that we will worship a golden calf in the open. It is that we will worship comfort quietly, while calling it responsibility.

## Name money as a rival, not a neutral

Jesus personifies wealth on purpose. Mammon is a master, and it competes for the seat that God alone should hold. The reason the comfortable rarely feel the danger is that the idol of money does not announce itself. It works through reasonable-sounding things: planning, security, providing, getting ahead. None of those are evil. But underneath them can run a quiet trust that says, if I have enough, I am safe, which is a confession that your real security is in the account and not in God.

The test is simple and uncomfortable. What threatens your peace most? For many of us it is not the state of our soul but the state of our finances, and that ranking tells you which master is actually in charge.

## Generosity is the lever that breaks money's grip

Jesus prescribes a specific medicine for the love of money, and it is not guilt. It is giving. Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also, he said, and the order matters. Move the treasure and the heart follows. You do not become free from money's grip by feeling bad about wealth. You become free by giving it away, regularly and sacrificially, until the open hand is simply the shape of how you live.

This is why the early church gave so radically that, Luke says, there was not a needy person among them. They had discovered that generosity is not a tax on the rich but a rescue for the rich, a way of loosening a grip that would otherwise harden the heart. Give first, before life bends the giving down. Give enough to feel it. And give in secret, so the giving works on your heart and not your reputation.

## Refuse both tribes' money gospels

The affluent society offers two false gospels of money, and the church has baptized both. One says that wealth is a sign of God's favor and your own virtue, that prosperity is the reward of the faithful. That is a lie the prophets would have torched. The other says that money is dirty and the spiritual person despises it and the system that produces it. That is its own kind of pride, often held by people quite comfortable. The ancient Christian ethic refuses both. It says wealth is a gift and a danger, that the rich are not heroes and not villains but stewards under judgment, and that the question is never how much you have but whose you are and whose it is.

Do not let a party tell you whether your money is a trophy or a crime. Let Scripture tell you it is a trust, on loan, to be handled with open hands and a sober heart.

## Contentment is the quiet rebellion

Paul learned the secret of being content in plenty and in want, and called it a secret because the affluent society works tirelessly to keep us from it. The whole machine runs on discontent, on the conviction that you need the next thing to be complete. Contentment is the quiet rebellion against that machine. Godliness with contentment, Paul says, is great gain. The person who has learned to say enough has escaped a treadmill that most of the rich will run until they die.

I have run that treadmill, telling myself the next acquisition was the responsible one. It never was the last one. The treadmill does not have a last one. Only contentment gets you off it.

## This week

Look honestly at what threatens your peace most, and ask whether money has taken a seat that belongs to God. Then do one concrete thing to loosen its grip: give something away that you will actually feel, in secret, this week. And practice one act of contentment, refusing one purchase the machine has convinced you that you need. Move the treasure, and watch the heart begin, slowly, to follow.
